name: Esther Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a bulldozer at an open-cut coal mine, pushing overburden, which is the dirt and rock on top of the coal, so the draglines and shovels can get at the seam. Most of the day is shaping benches and cleaning up after the blasts, slow careful work where an inch matters. I'm still learning to read the ground, and the trainer, Marco, sits in with me once a week and tells me I'm too heavy on the blade. I like that it's honest work you can see at the end of the shift.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does life look like outside the mine?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Priya, she's a graphic designer who works from home. No kids. The pay's high, and I've got about eight months saved plus some shares I've been buying since I started. I'm also doing an online diploma in automation, mostly at night, with an AI tutor on my laptop. Plenty of mines around here, though they're mostly coal, which is its own problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So AI fizzles. Fine by me, but coal still has a closing date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI was oversold, sure, but I'd also say the real change in coal was never about AI. It's climate. Our mine has a closure date in about nine years, and I'd keep saying the government should plan for that properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my dozer job lasts until the mine closes, not longer. Our coal mine has a closing date in nine years, and no AI plateau changes that for anyone on my crew. So I'd still need a plan B, just a slower one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep dozing, keep the diploma going at night, and keep buying shares every month. I'd look at moving to a metals mine in the next few years, because copper and lithium are growing. I'd still use the AI tutor every day, plateau or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not about AI, about coal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Priya feel about the closing date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd move anywhere with good internet, so she's relaxed. I'm the one who'd have to find a new mine. It's not urgent, but it's always there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything AI would still change in your day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the survey maps on my screen get updated faster. That would actually help me, because I'd stop pushing to old lines. It's small but it'd save me from Marco's comments.

The government should plan properly for our **mine's closure** date.
think: Her dozer job lasts until the **mine closes** in about nine years.
She still needs a **plan B**, just a slower one.
do: Keep the **automation diploma** going at night.
Look at moving to a **metals mine** in the next few years.
feel: **A bit uneasy**, about coal rather than AI.

fieldNote: Her worry comes from **coal's closure date**, which no plateau removes.

steps.text: Keep studying the automation diploma at night
Buy shares every month from her pay
Apply to copper or lithium mines within three years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the one I've been studying for, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it at work: this is where miners who learn the systems get ahead, and the union should demand training for everyone. Online I'd share stuff about autonomous fleets and say workers should be part of the rollout, not victims of it. With friends I'd be pretty upbeat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's good for me. Planning and survey work get automated first, and they'll need people on the ground who understand both the machine and the software. I'm a bad dozer driver but a good student, so a mine full of software might actually suit me better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to join the autonomous dozer trial or the remote ops pilot straight away. I'd finish the diploma within the year and get the automation certificate. And I'd keep investing, maybe in a mining tech fund, because I believe in where it's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly. A little guilty about being excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why guilty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Marco, my trainer, has thirty years on dozers and doesn't want to learn any of it. When I'm excited, it's partly at his expense. I'd want the company to look after people like him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone on your crew who's scared?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn one system, any system. I'd show them how I use the AI tutor to study. Most of them have never tried it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that's a different level. Two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a basic income or a big transition package, now, not after. I'd go online and push for that. At work I'd say the union has to bargain hard before the robots arrive in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the diploma I'm doing might be outdated before I finish it. If AI can do all the thinking by 2028, it can also program the robots. An automation diploma made sense in 2026, but with AGI by 2028 the AI could be writing the robot code itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the diploma anyway, fast, and go for whatever hands-on maintenance work the robots need. I'd move more savings into cash and shares in the companies making the robots. I'd keep the dozer until 2031 and bank every pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'm not frozen. I'd be moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The dozer's hands-on, so I'd probably keep it until 2031. My study plan is thinking work, so that's hit on day one. Weirdly, the old job is the safer one for those three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Priya talk about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Her design work goes in 2028, mine maybe in 2031. So I'd be the earner for a while, and we'd need to be careful. We might move somewhere cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years plus three. I could do a lot with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where governments really have to show up. Training for everyone, and taxes on the companies that save money with robots. I'd keep sharing that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think I can get into the robot maintenance side by 2030 and be one of the people the mine keeps. Five years is enough for me to stop being the worst dozer driver and become the person who fixes the dozers that drive themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the diploma in year one, then ask for a move to the autonomous systems team. Keep investing monthly. Maybe move to a lithium mine if coal is closing anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way. Mostly I'd feel ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robots might be fixed by other robots by then. I don't know. I'd keep an eye on that and keep my savings strong just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay in mining at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, because I like being outside. But if the money's in software, I'd be flexible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37 when the robots get good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do a fair transition here, and I'd want the coal towns at the front of the line. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen. Online I'd keep it positive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm fine. Ten years gives me time to finish my diploma, get a metals mine job and still be young when the robots arrive. I'd also be watching for what the next thing is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the diploma, move to a metals mine within a few years, and keep investing. I'd probably try AI tools at work every day. Maybe buy a house with Priya too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a long road, but a clear one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you see yourself in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe running a team that looks after autonomous trucks. Or teaching others. I'd like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything still worrying you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The coal towns. They've had it rough already with climate rules, and they'd need a lot of help. I'd volunteer if there was a local group.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my whole plan becomes outdated before I finish it. What would help is a government transition package, paid training and a basic income floor. I've done everything right for the slow future, and the fast one would still catch me halfway through my diploma.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the climate side. For coal miners, AI is the second wave, not the first.

headlineQuote: I've done everything right for the slow future, and the fast one would still catch me halfway through my diploma.
portrait: Esther is a **27-year-old** dozer operator at an open-cut coal mine, still learning to read the ground.
She lives with Priya, a graphic designer, and has **eight months saved** plus shares.
She studies **automation** at night with an AI tutor and uses AI tools every day.
She sees coal's **closure date** as her first threat, and AI as the second.
She's **calm** in slower scenarios but **anxious** when AGI arrives by 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her automation diploma could be outdated before she finishes it.
whatWouldHelp: A government **transition package**, paid training and a **basic income** floor.
